extraction.name: WebWalkerQA
extraction.description: WebWalkerQA is a benchmark designed to assess the ability of LLMs to perform web traversal. It evaluates the capacity of LLMs to traverse a website’s subpages to extract high-quality data systematically. It is composed of 680 question-answer pairs from four real-world scenarios across over 1373 webpages, including both single-source and multi-source QAs in English and Chinese.
extraction.creator: Jialong Wu, Wenbiao Yin, Yong Jiang, Zhenglin Wang, Zekun Xi, Runnan Fang, Linhai Zhang, Yulan He, Deyu Zhou, Pengjun Xie, Fei Huang
extraction.citeAs: Wu, Jialong; Yin, Wenbiao; Jiang, Yong; Wang, Zhenglin; Xi, Zekun; Fang, Runnan; Zhang, Linhai; He, Yulan; Zhou, Deyu; Xie, Pengjun; Huang, Fei. WebWalker: Benchmarking LLMs in Web Traversal. arXiv:2501.07572.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed with a two-stage funnel annotation strategy combining LLM-based and human annotation. First, root official websites across conference, organization, education, and game domains were collected. Then the authors recursively traversed official websites, collecting accessible sub-links and their pages. GPT-4o generated synthetic QA pairs based on gathered information using predefined rules for single-source and multi-source settings. Finally, crowd-sourced human annotators rewrote, calibrated, verified, and filtered the questions and answers to ensure correctness, consistency, accuracy, and relevance.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from official websites in four domains: conference, organization, education, and game. The root page was initially identified through a Google search using keywords such as "conference official website" or "game official website," followed by manual filtering. For the education domain, official websites of various university computer science departments were chosen. The collected raw page content included webpage markdown-like content and clickable HTML buttons and associated URLs extracted from pages.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The construction process included generating synthetic QA pairs from collected subpages, verifying and filtering legitimate queries, retaining only QA pairs with short answers containing entities, and rewriting and calibrating questions and answers by human annotators. The final annotated JSON format includes Question, Answer, Root_Url, and Info fields such as Hop, Domain, Language, Difficulty_Level, Source Website, and Golden_Path.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Official websites were recursively traversed to collect accessible sub-links and pages. Web pages were obtained in a Markdown-like format, and clickable HTML buttons with corresponding URLs were extracted using Beautiful Soup. Queries were constructed from page information, then QA pairs were verified and filtered to remove unnatural phrasing and non-concise answers, keeping only short-answer entity-style QA pairs.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation used a two-stage process. In the first stage, GPT-4o performed initial annotation by generating question-answer pairs from collected webpage information for both multi-source and single-source settings using detailed prompts. In the second stage, crowd-sourced human annotators conducted quality control and filtering, and could rewrite and calibrate the questions and answers to ensure the QA pairs were correct and consistent. For multi-source annotation, questions had to require combining information from at least two sublinks; for single-source annotation, current knowledge from one document had to be required. Strict verification prompts were used to judge whether generated QA pairs met criteria.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper describes strict verification and filtering of synthetic QA pairs. Generated queries were checked for whether they could be accurately answered from the intended documents, whether answers were concise entity or judgment types, whether both documents were necessary for multi-source questions, and whether phrasing was natural. Human annotators then rewrote and calibrated questions and answers to ensure correctness and consistency.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that the WebWalkerQA dataset will be available at HuggingFace Datasets and that the code of WebWalker will be released on GitHub.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work highlights the importance of deep, vertical exploration in web-based tasks and aims to improve scalable and reliable LLM-based information retrieval integrated with RAG. The benchmark is intended to evaluate and improve information-seeking over authoritative official websites in real-world scenarios.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently comprises 680 high-quality QA pairs due to the complexity of web-agent queries. The authors note they also have approximately 14k silver QA pairs that are not yet carefully human-verified. The work only utilizes HTML-DOM to parse clickable buttons and does not include visual modalities such as screenshots. WebWalker is driven by prompting without additional training. The benchmark is built on official websites with dynamically updated information, and experiments show that search engines and RAG systems struggle to retrieve deeply buried content. The paper also notes that as depth or number of sources increases, task difficulty rises and accuracy declines.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs’ web traversal abilities in complex, multi-step information-seeking tasks. It is used to assess question-answering accuracy and action efficiency of web agents and RAG systems, including single-source and multi-source QA evaluation across domains and languages. The paper also notes that approximately 14k silver QA pairs may serve as supplementary training data to enhance agent performance.
